grades.quote: demonstrate a program continuing to make use of an open file after all names for that file have been removed.
grades.reason: Only an exercise prompt (8.10) asking the reader to demonstrate a program still using an open file after all its names are removed. It shows the phenomenon exists but does not explain why it happens.

grades.quote: iput() doesn’t truncate a file immediately when the link count for the file drops to zero, because some process might still hold a reference to the inode in memory: a process might still be reading and writing to the file, because
grades.reason: Explains the mechanism. When the link count reaches zero, iput() does not truncate the file, because a process that already opened it may still hold a reference and keep reading or writing it. The rest of the passage covers crash recovery, which is auxiliary.

grades.quote: The unlink system call removes a name from the file system. The file’s inode and the disk space holding its content are only freed when the file’s link count is zero and no file descriptors refer to it.
grades.reason: States directly why content remains accessible after unlink. unlink removes only a name, and the inode and data are freed only when the link count is zero and no file descriptors refer to it. It also shows that the file stays accessible under another link.

grades.quote: is an idiomatic way to create a temporary inode with no name that will be cleaned up when the process closes fd or exits.
grades.reason: Gives the open-then-unlink idiom. The file stays usable through the open fd as an unnamed temporary inode until the fd is closed or the process exits. This shows the behavior and hints at the reason, but it is brief and not a full explanation.
